extracted.intended_audience: geometers, students of Euclid's Elements, and editors/commentators of classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the definitions (what counts as 'given') from Euclid's Data together with the editor's notes about correct demonstration, construction, and editorial practice in Euclid's Elements. Emphasizes how to treat assumptions, constructions, translations, and omitted steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I — 'given' in magnitude (spaces, lines, angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spaces, lines, and angles, are said to be given in magnitude, when equals to them can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To treat a space/line/angle as 'given in magnitude' one must be able to exhibit or find an equal magnitude; demonstrating equality by exhibiting a constructible equal suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II — 'given' ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: A ratio is said to be given, when a ratio of a given magnitude to a given magnitude which is the same ratio with it can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a ratio is given, produce two given magnitudes whose ratio equals the target ratio (i.e., reduce to a ratio of known/given magnitudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III — rectilineal figures given in species
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectilineal figures are said to be given in species, which have each of their angles given, and the ratios of their sides given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A polygon is 'given in species' when its angles are known and the side-length ratios are given; use these data when transforming between equivalent figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV — 'given' in position (points, lines, spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Points, lines, and spaces, are said to be given in position, which have always the same situation, and which are either actually exhibited, or can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To treat geometric elements as given in position they must be fixed/locatable (either drawn/exhibited or constructible by known steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition A — angle given in position
rubrics_metrics.description: An angle is said to be given in position which is contained by straight lines given in position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An angle inherits 'given in position' status from its bounding lines; ensure those lines are given/locatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition V — circle given in magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle is said to be given in magnitude, when a straight line from its centre to the circumference is given in magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circle's givenness in magnitude is determined by its radius (centre-to-circumference); provide or find that radius to treat the circle as given in magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VI — circle given in position and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle is said to be given in position and magnitude, the centre of which is given in position, and a straight line from it to the circumference is given in magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the centre's position and the radius magnitude must be known/exhibited to call a circle given in position and magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VII — segments of circles given in magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments of circles are said to be given in magnitude, when the angles in them, and their bases, are given in magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To consider a circular segment given in magnitude, ensure its central/inscribed angles and the base chord lengths are given in magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VIII — segments of circles given in position and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments of circles are said to be given in position and magnitude, when the angles in them are given in magnitude, and their bases are given both in position and magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires both magnitude data (angles) and positional/magnitude data of bases (chords) to be considered fully given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IX — 'greater by a given magnitude'
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnitude is said to be greater than another by a given magnitude, when this given magnitude being taken from it, the Remainder is equal to the other magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assert one magnitude exceeds another by a given amount, demonstrate that subtracting the given amount yields equality; this provides a constructive criterion for 'greater by'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition X — 'less by a given magnitude'
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnitude is said to be less than another by a given magnitude, when this given magnitude being added to it, the whole is equal to the other magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assert 'less by', show adding the given magnitude produces equality; this is the constructive test for 'less by'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Demonstrating that something is 'given' (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: In proofs of the Data, to show a magnitude or ratio is 'given' it is sufficient to find one or more equal magnitudes (or a fourth proportional when required) which are themselves given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the propositions: to show A/B is given, find C and D equal to A and B respectively; to show a part is given, subtract or add a given magnitude to exhibit equality; to show ratios between composed magnitudes, use composition/conversion with given ratios. The supplied reasoning repeatedly uses the method 'exhibit equals' or 'find a fourth proportional' to establish givenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of existential assumptions in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrations of theorems it is sufficient that a thing made use of in the reasoning can possibly exist, provided this be evident, though it cannot be exhibited or found by a geometrical construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor notes that for some steps (e.g., 'there may be a fourth proportional' or 'there is some square equal to the circle') one may legitimately assume existence if it is evident, even when a geometric construction to exhibit it is not available; but this should be made explicit and justified, not silently assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Do not grant propositions without demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions such as 'ratios that are triplicate of ratios equal to one another are likewise the same with one another' ought not to be granted without a demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposition generalizes an already-proved duplicate case (e.g., duplicate ratios) to a higher power (triplicate), provide a demonstration analogous to the proved case (Euclid proved duplicates, so give a proof for triplicates rather than assume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Provide constructions when solids/figures are asserted to have properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When solids are said to be equiangular or a solid polyhedron is to be described in another sphere similar to one already described, the construction by which these are made/described must be given (not merely assumed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming geometric objects 'already made' and properties of their solid angles; either give the construction or justify applicability of a prior legitimate construction (e.g., use earlier corollary that renders a later demonstration legitimate if solids are constructed as in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Demonstrate intermediate geometric facts that are invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof relies on auxiliary geometric facts (e.g., that triangles/pyramids formed by dividing polygonal bases are similar, or that bisectors of opposite planes lie in one plane), these facts ought to be explicitly demonstrated rather than asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes repeatedly correct demonstrations that omitted necessary checks: show similarity of triangular pyramids when basing ratios on them; prove coplanarity of bisectors instead of assuming it; supply lemmas where editors left crucial steps out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Avoid mutilation/equivocation in demonstrations and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations should not be 'spoiled and mutilated' by overly explicit treatment of trivial steps while omitting less obvious necessary steps; figure labels must be consistent with the text and steps (e.g., ensure perpendicular falls on the intended point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the figure and the verbal construction carefully (e.g., don't say 'draw KC2 from K perpendicular to BD' when you must 'join KV' and demonstrate that KA^ is perpendicular to BD). Correct inconsistent labeling (same point marked with two letters) and supply missed lemmas where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Omit redundant repetition and mark editorial insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'in like manner we may demonstrate' should be omitted when they merely repeat a demonstration already given; their presence may indicate later editorial additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a step is literally the same as a prior demonstration, avoid repeating it verbatim; when such repetitive phrases appear without necessity, treat them as likely editorial insertions and consider removing or annotating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Translate and refer Greek wording carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations must map Greek phrases to their correct referents so the English enunciation matches the intended geometric meaning (e.g., do not misplace which clauses refer to which spheres or solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating enunciations, test the translated meaning against the required construction and figure: words that appear to refer to one object in some translations may properly refer to another according to the proposition's logic and figure; adjust translation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Corrections by editors should restore Euclid's order and remove spurious additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should restore the order of letters, remove propositions improperly inserted near the end with no connection, and correct errors introduced by unskilful editors to bring the Elements nearer to Euclid's original accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check alphabetic/letter order in propositions, remove or annotate propositions that are disconnected, and supply omitted demonstrations or lemmas to remedy 'blemishes' introduced by later editors; cite earlier authorities (Clavius, Dee, Commandine) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Use of prior propositions and definitions in shorter demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever possible, use previously demonstrated propositions (e.g., prop. 21 B.6 or 10 B.11) to give shorter demonstrations; avoid unnecessary repetition of results already established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes shorten many proofs by citing earlier propositions; adopt this practice to streamline proofs, but ensure the cited proposition legitimately applies to the present case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — When lemmas are annexed they must clarify, not obscure
rubrics_metrics.description: Added lemmas (by editors) should explain omitted steps; a spurious lemma which explains nothing may indicate the editor failed to understand the original proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an editor's added lemma does not resolve the omitted point, rewrite or replace it with a correct lemma/demonstration that makes the reasoning clear.
